transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2025-05-22
- Time: 16:00 PDT
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos & Jill (Redwood SEs), Kevin (CSM), Liang, Sara, Tom, Priya (Aperture)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping to align on success criteria, workload sizing, required capacity (reserved GPUs), autoscale/burst behavior, and benchmark plan/timeline. Customer wants predictable tail latency under load and cost constraints; interested in reserved capacity + burst to hosted/dedicated fallback policies.

Topics:
- High-level success criteria (p50/p95 latency targets, throughput, error budget)
- Workload profiling (RPS, token lengths, concurrency, KV cache locality)
- POC capacity: reserved baseline, burst pool, scaling window & cooldowns
- Fallback policies: model variant routing, regional failover, queued requests vs best-effort
- Benchmarks & timelines, security docs needed

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you carving out the time. Quick intros please?
[00:10] Liang (Customer): Hi Liang here, staff ML eng, I own model infra for NLU.
[00:14] Sara: Sara, platform eng, I'll handle networking and infra constraints.
[00:18] Tom: Tom, head of AI, here to sign off on success criteria.
[00:22] Priya: Priya, security. I'll need SOC2/ISO and KMS details.
[00:26] Carlos (SE): Carlos from Redwood, I'll lead the technical plan for capacity and benchmarks.
[00:31] Jill (SE): Jill supporting on orchestration and autoscale config.
[00:34] Kevin (CSM): Kevin, CSM, will help with timelines and onboarding.

[02:05] Maya: Goal for today's call is to scope a POC: what baseline reserved capacity you need, how much burst we allow, what success looks like. Can you run through your current traffic profile?
[02:20] Liang: Sure, current prod-ish traffic for the NLU endpoint is ~120 RPS peak, average ~40 RPS. Payloads vary; avg input length around 150 tokens, tail up to 800 tokens for some long-form parsing. Latency expectations: product team wants p50 < 150ms and p95 < 500ms for typical shorter requests, but for long-form we can accept p95 ~1.2s.
[02:52] Sara: Also, we run from a single cloud region us-west-2 and we can't do cross-region fallbacks without a compliance review. Network egress limits are reasonable. We can open VPC peering and provide a private endpoint.
[03:15] Tom: Cost is a factor — we'd prefer reserved monthly capacity to keep unit costs predictable, but we need burst when marketing spikes happen.

[05:00] Carlos: Good, that helps. For POC we usually pick a reserved baseline that covers about 60-70% of expected peak so the burst pool covers spikes. With your 120 RPS peak, baseline 70-80 RPS reserved makes sense, then allow burst up to 180-200 RPS depending on GPU shapes. Do you have a preferred GPU or are you open to Redwood recommending?
[05:28] Liang: We don't have infra preference, open to your recommendation; we run mixed workloads so quantization/FP16 is fine.

[06:00] Jill: For latency targets, the GPU type and batching will dominate. If we run on 4xA100 equivalent with continuous batching and KV cache enabled, short requests (150 tokens) should hit p50 ~60-120ms and p95 ~300-400ms depending on batching window. Longer requests will be higher. We can give concrete numbers in the benchmark plan.

[07:10] Priya: On security — we need SOC2 Type II, SAML SSO, KMS integration and audit logs. Also clarify data retention for logs.
[07:25] Kevin: We'll share the security pack; Redwood supports customer-managed KMS in Private deployments and can produce audit logs. For hosted we have retention options.

[08:00] Liang: For the POC success criteria: 1) p95 under 500ms for <= 200 token requests at 100 RPS sustained; 2) graceful degradation under spikes where latency for long-form can increase but no error rate >1%; 3) throughput stability for 3 hours of sustained traffic. Does that sound reasonable?
[08:28] Carlos: Yes that aligns. We'll run two configurations: 1) Dedicated reserved baseline (4xA100 equiv) sized to 80 RPS; 2) Burst policy to add up to 2 additional nodes to hit 180-200 RPS. We'll measure p50/p95, tail latency, GPU utilization, and per-token cost.

[10:40] Maya: How fast does autoscale need to react? What about cooldowns?
[10:46] Jill: Autoscale strategy: warm reserved pool always on; burst pool cold/warm — we recommend a hybrid: keep minimal warm capacity for small bursts and allow rapid cold starts for larger bursts with a queued/fallback policy. For POC we can simulate both: immediate burst up to 20% via warm instances, and measurable cold start latency for spin-up to full burst capacity. Cooldown we typically configure at 90s to 300s depending on request distribution.
[11:20] Liang: Cold start latency worries me. If we spin new GPUs that's minutes.
[11:26] Carlos: Correct, cold start of new hardware can be minutes; to mitigate we do instance pre-warming and can use multi-tier fallback: 1) serve with a smaller quantized model variant on existing capacity (faster inference), 2) queue requests with progress responses, or 3) overflow to hosted region if allowed. For your compliance constraints, option 1 (model variant fallback) is safest.
[12:05] Tom: What's the expected quality delta when falling back to a smaller model?
[12:12] Jill: Small quantized variant usually preserves top-level intents well; we should validate using your eval set. We'll include quality regression checks in the benchmark. If quality drop is unacceptable, we can earmark more reserved capacity or a faster warm pool.

[14:00] Maya: For the POC benchmark plan we propose: 1) Baseline runs at 80 RPS sustained for 3 hours; 2) Step load up to 180 RPS to observe autoscale and burst; 3) Spike tests (short 5-minute blasts to 250 RPS) to test fallback behavior; 4) Long-form requests sub-test for 800-token tails. We'll collect p50/p90/p95, GPU util, token cost, error rate, cold start times.
[14:30] Liang: That looks good. We'll provide a sample of 500 requests with token distribution and 30 minutes of real traffic logs so you can shape the load.

[16:10] Priya: For security docs, we'll need data flow diagrams and KMS key usage details. Also confirm whether PII is logged and where.
[16:22] Kevin: We'll include the security pack and a runbook for the POC that shows data residency and logs.

[18:00] Carlos: A quick note on caching: if you have strong prefix locality, Redwood's prefix/KV cache can reduce downstream compute by up to 40-60% for repetitive prompts; we'll measure cache hit rates during the POC. Please indicate if you have high reuse in prompts.
[18:20] Liang: We do have a lot of repeated system prompts and templated user prompts — caching should help.

[20:45] Maya: Budget/contracting question — you said cost matters. Typical POC pricing is a short-term reserved baseline discount plus a metered burst surcharge. We'll send two pricing options: monthly reserved commit with lower per-token cost and a no-commit pilot with on-demand rates for comparison.
[21:10] Tom: We prefer a short reserved pilot if the numbers make sense.

[22:00] Jill: On orchestration details: autoscaler metrics we'll use CPU/GPU util, queue length, and p95 latency rules. Scaling thresholds: scale-up when GPU util > 65% sustained for 30s or queue length > X, scale-down after util < 30% for 180s. For POC we can tune those thresholds.

[24:05] Liang: What about model parallelism and memory for 800-token requests?
[24:12] Carlos: For long sequences we'll use larger memory configs and limit batch sizes to avoid OOM; we can also shard KV cache across nodes. We'll capture mem pressure during runs.

[26:00] Priya: Any network egress or data residency issues with burst to hosted?
[26:10] Kevin: If burst spills to hosted region, we can restrict to same region; cross-region is blocked unless you sign off. We'll keep everything in us-west-2 for the POC.

[28:30] Liang: SLA — we need to define SLOs to decide success. For the POC, metric-based acceptance criteria are fine, but for production we'll need SLA items in contract.
[28:45] Maya: Understood — POC success criteria will be metric-based; we'll capture those and then work on production SLA as a next step.

[31:00] Tom: Timeline — we want to start POC end of month if possible. What do you think?
[31:08] Maya: If we get your sample data and approve networking by 2025-05-24 we can start the benchmark run as early as 2025-05-27 and finish initial analysis by 2025-06-02. That fits your window.

[33:20] Carlos: For the actual reserved GPU sizing — our recommendation for your workload is starting with 4xA100-equivalent reserved baseline. That gives headroom for 80 RPS with room for batching. Burst pool of 2x same nodes should reach ~180-200 RPS depending on batching and sequence length.
[33:45] Liang: Will quantization affect latency and cost significantly?
[33:52] Jill: Yes — 4-bit/8-bit quant profiles lower GPU mem and increase throughput. We'll test FP16 and int8-like profiles. For POC we'll validate quality vs cost tradeoffs.

[36:10] Maya: Can you confirm what we need from Aperture to run the bench?
[36:18] Liang: We'll share 500 request sample with token lengths, 30 minutes of traffic logs, network contact for VPC peering, and a list of IPs to allow. Also a person from platform to coordinate.

[38:00] Carlos: Redwood will provide a benchmark template, a runbook for access, and a short security packet. We'll also provide an estimated cost sheet for the reserved vs on-demand pilots.

[40:05] Priya: We'll need a redacted data sample for security review; can the data be stored ephemeral only for the run?
[40:12] Kevin: Yes, retention can be configured; logs can be purged after the run per your request. We'll include retention settings in the runbook.

[42:15] Tom: A couple of small asks — include a regression test on quality comparing the fallback model and the full model, and include per-token cost breakdown so we can present to finance.
[42:30] Carlos: We'll add per-token cost and quality regression columns in the benchmark report.

[44:40] Maya: Recap and next steps: 1) Aperture to share sample requests + network details by 2025-05-24; 2) Redwood to send pricing and contract by 2025-05-23; 3) Redwood to run POC starting ~2025-05-27; 4) Follow-up meeting week of 2025-06-02 to review results.

[46:00] Liang: Sounds good. One more thing — do you have references of similar customers?
[46:10] Maya: We can share a couple of anonymized case studies, and we have internal benchmarks (we'll include them in the deck).

[48:30] Priya: Okay that's it from security. Thanks.
[48:35] Maya: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with the items and links.

Action items (in transcript):
- Maya: Send pricing, pilot contract draft, and case studies by 2025-05-23.
- Carlos: Share benchmark template, runbook, and S3 link; coordinate test dataset access by 2025-05-24.
- Liang: Provide sample requests, traffic logs, and platform contact by 2025-05-24.
- Priya: Provide compliance questions and confirm retention preferences by 2025-05-24.

Links referenced:

- Security pack / SOC2 doc (will be shared)

End of transcript.
